newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Africa finally gets privatisation bug.
newsitem.headline: Africa finally gets privatisation bug.

text.p: Compared to Latin America and Eastern Europe, Africa is a privatisation laggard.

But the world's poorest continent is becoming aware of the advantages of a process which can inject badly-needed capital and technology, according to officials and industry experts attending the first pan-African privatisation conference.
Governments from the Cape to Cairo are keen to sell state assets to cut state debt and boost industrial efficiency, using foreign cash and know-how.
"Coming out of their previous anti-market orientation, Africa and its leaders have rediscovered the benefits of foreign direct investment," said Ken Kwaku of the World Bank.

North Africa has seen most of the recent action with the Egyptian government floating 14 companies between May and August and Morocco last year offering 35 percent of shares in steel producer Sonasid.

South of the Sahara progress has been slower. The reform lobby suffered a setback in January this year when Nigeria's military government rowed back on earlier promises of major privatisations, saying the issue needed more study.
Nonetheless there is tangible progress in several countries and officials acknowledge the central role of private capital.

"The productive sector must be handled by the private sector because that is where the motivation is, that is where the incentives are and that is where the growth is," said Ugandan Finance Minister Matthew Rukikaire.

Zambia, the continent's foremost pioneer of privatisation, moves into a critical phase this year with the sale of Zambian Consolidated Copper Mines, the mining giant which accounts for about 90 percent of export earnings.

Ghana, Kenya, Uganda, the Ivory Coast, Uganda and Mozambique are among other countries that have already taken notable privatisation steps while Tanzania plans to sell 128 state-owned enterprises by the end of 1997.
The continent's economic giant, South Africa, has been slower to embrace the concept, with African National Congress politicians only recently prepared to use the "P" word.

But the mood here has changed, too, with the imminent sale of a 30 percent stake in telecoms group Telkom to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium for an estimated $1 billion plus, the biggest sub-Saharan privatisation yet.
Public Enterprises Minister Stella Sigcau said Pretoria was now embarked on the largest and most far-reaching of restructuring of state assets on the African continent.
Mozambican Prime Minister Pascoal Mocumbi told the conference that privatisation was "a basic component of reactivating the national economy".
It was a sentiment echoed by other officials from governments and international institutions, although not uniformly on the ground.

For African opponents, privatisation is another element of the harsh structural ajustment programmes which have proved controversial across the continent, while for organised labour -- particularly vocal in South Africa -- it spells job cuts.
The World Bank's Kwaku acknowledged local opposition but said the gains for Africa will be substantial, helping suck in capital which has so far largely passed the continent by.
During 1995, net foreign direct investment into developing countries was about $97 billion, of which Africa received a mere $3 billion.

"Privatisations have played a key role in reducing the indebtedness of Latin American countries in the past 15 years or so. Their prospects can be no different in Africa if we muster the political will and commitment," Kwaku said.
